title: Hearts not yet soft?
hookLine: has the time not come for believers' hearts to humble themselves (57:16)

lines: A ROBBER ON A WALL AT NIGHT.
A VERSE FROM A NEARBY HOUSE.
YES, LORD, THE TIME HAS COME.
cards: There's a story told about a man named Fudayl ibn 'Iyad. In his youth, the story goes, he was a highway robber.
One night he was climbing a wall to meet someone he shouldn't, and from a house nearby he heard a voice reciting the Qur'an. One verse, a question.
He stopped on the wall and answered it out loud: yes, Lord, the time has come. He climbed down a different man, and the story remembers him afterward as an ascetic and a teacher.

teach.b: Surah Al-Hadid, verse sixteen. Pickthall: "Is not the time ripe for the hearts of those who believe to submit to Allah's reminder and to the truth which is revealed".
It opens: alam ya'ni lilladhina amanu an takhsha'a qulubuhum. Notice who's asked. Not unbelievers: those who believe, people who already pray and already know the words.
Has the time not come for their hearts to soften? The verb is takhsha'a, from khushu', the humble stillness meant to fill prayer.

teach.h: KHUSHU': A HEART THAT STOPS RESISTING.
teach.b: A heart with khushu' has stopped resisting.
Sahih Muslim preserves a striking line from the companion Ibn Mas'ud: between the time they accepted Islam and the time God reproached them with this verse, there were only four years.
Four years in, and already the question: have you gotten used to it? The verse warns against hearts that grow hard as time stretches on.

teach.h: THE EARTH REVIVED AFTER ITS DEATH.
teach.b: Then the next verse offers the turn: know that God brings the earth back to life after its death. A dead field after rain.
Commentators read the two together: hardness isn't permanent, and a heart can be revived the way the ground is.

Read that way, the Fudayl story, whatever its historical details, is the next verse acted out: a hard heart turned over in one night. And the question has no date written on it. It stays open, for whoever hears it.

how: Muslim preachers and teachers often recite 57:16 as a call to renewed sincerity, and the story of Fudayl ibn 'Iyad's turning is widely told in sermons and books on repentance.

o: fear of the punishment waiting on the Last Day
the bowing position in the daily prayer
humble stillness; a heart that stops resisting

games.q: the question in Al-Hadid — tap the pairs.
p: heard the verse from a wall

s: the verse is addressed to unbelievers
it asks those who believe whether the time has come for their hearts to soften.
Ibn Mas'ud said the reproach came only four years after they accepted Islam
the next verse speaks of the earth revived after its death
commentators read it as hope: a hard heart can be revived.

games.q: you're Fudayl, halfway up a wall at night, and you hear the verse: has the time not come? what do you do?
o: keep climbing; it's just a voice.
answer it: yes, Lord, the time has come.
go home and think about it next year.
games.why: in the story people tell, he answered out loud, climbed down, and turned his life around.

practice: Notice where you hold tension, jaw, shoulders, hands, and let it soften.
Then hold one place your heart has gone hard, a grudge, a habit you've stopped noticing, a person you've stopped listening to, without fixing it, and ask quietly: has the time not come?
On each out-breath, let a little of it loosen.

wordCard.voice: Khushu': the humble stillness of a softened heart, which Surah Al-Hadid asks believers whether the time has come to have. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: has the time not come for those who believe? ya'ni means it has become time, it is ripe.

carryVoice: Your line: has the time not come? Hard ground comes back after rain. That's day six hundred thirteen.
